diagnostic_evidence.quote: \phi\bigl(r_{ij}^\varepsilon(t)\bigr) \bigl(c_j(t)-c_i(t)\bigr), \quad t \in (0,T],
Here $\phi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is a differentiable interaction kernel that weighs the influence of neighbouring agents
$T$ should be large enough to enable the formation of clusters -- or, in the language of opinion dynamics, to let the agents reach consensus.

issues.failure_explanation: For any differentiable (locally Lipschitz) kernel that is positive on the relevant range, as required for attractive interaction, the dynamics (1) is a smooth ODE and pairwise differences never vanish at finite time: e.g. for two interacting agents d/dt(c_1-c_2) = -phi(r_12)(c_1-c_2) with bounded continuous coefficient, whose solution decays exponentially and is nonzero for every finite t (pixel positions are distinct, so r_12 stabilises at a positive value where phi>0). Exact clusters (piecewise-constant quantization) are therefore reached only asymptotically as t -> infinity, not 'in finite time'.

failure_location.quote: Classical results for opinion dynamics models~\cite{MotschTadmor2014} ensure that, under mild assumptions on $\phi$, the solution converges to a finite number of clusters in finite time.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace 'in finite time' by 'asymptotically (exponentially fast) as t -> infinity', or state the extra kernel hypotheses (e.g. a dead zone at the origin) actually needed for finite-time clustering.
issues.overall_effect: The stated guarantee that the dynamics produces an exact colour quantization at a finite time, the premise for reading the state at a finite horizon T as a segmented image, is unreliable; clustering at finite T holds only approximately.
issues.title: Claimed finite-time convergence to clusters is false for the model's smooth dynamics
issues.why_classification: A one-clause correction of a prose claim; no formal result, algorithm, or experiment depends on exact finite-time clustering, and the method, conclusions and scope all survive.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: \tilde J(c,\lambda,\varepsilon) = \int_0^T \int_\Omega \lambda(x,t) \cdot [\partial_t c(x,t) - F(c(x,t), \varepsilon(t))]\ dx\ dt + J(c(\,\cdot\, ,T; \varepsilon)).
=\int_\Omega \lambda(x,T)\, v(x,T)\ dx -  \int_\Omega \int_0^T [- \partial_t\lambda - \partial_c F(c,\varepsilon) \cdot \lambda]\, v\ dt dx
+ \int_\Omega  [-\Delta c(x,T) + \alpha (c(x,T) - I) ]\, v(x,T) dx,
\lambda (x,T) = -\Delta c(x,T) + \alpha (c(x,T) - I(x)).
\lambda(x,T) = - \rho \Delta u(x) + \dive(\mu(x) + \rho\, v(x) ) + \alpha (u(x) - I(x)), \quad x \in \Omega.

issues.failure_explanation: The first variation of the augmented functional (8) with respect to c, integrating by parts in t and x (with v(x,0)=0 and Neumann conditions), yields the terminal condition lambda(x,T) = Delta c(x,T) - alpha(c(x,T)-I(x)) = -J'(c(.,T)). Equation (10b) states the opposite sign. Indeed the appendix's own displayed identity has terminal terms +Int lambda(T)v + Int(-Delta c + alpha(c-I))v, which force lambda(T) = Delta c(T) - alpha(c(T)-I), contradicting the conclusion drawn immediately after; the appendix's middle term is also sign-erroneous (a correct integration by parts gives -Int[partial_t lambda + (partial_c F)^* lambda]v, not -Int[-partial_t lambda - partial_c F . lambda]v). Because the adjoint equation is homogeneous, the sign slip flips the whole adjoint and hence the search direction D = partial_eps F . lambda used by both algorithms; the same slip is repeated in the terminal condition (20) for the ADMM variant and determines the correct direction of the variational inequalities in the convergence remark.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Redo the integration by parts correctly and either flip the terminal condition in (10b) (and correspondingly in (20) and the convergence remark) to lambda = Delta c - alpha(c-I), or else explicitly adopt the opposite (Pontryagin-style) multiplier convention and then consistently reverse the sign of the update direction in the algorithms (see ISSUE-003).
issues.overall_effect: The derivation of the optimality system (9) is invalid as written and the stated system is inconsistent with the Lagrangian (8) from which it is supposedly derived; the adjoint computed in Algorithm 1 (and, via (20), in Algorithm 2) has a sign that, combined with ISSUE-003, makes the computed direction an ascent direction, and the sign of the variational-inequality stopping tests is likewise unreliable.
issues.title: Adjoint terminal condition in the optimality system has the wrong sign relative to its derivation
issues.why_classification: The repair requires redoing a variational inference that is presently erroneous and self-contradictory, and propagating the sign consistently through the optimality system, the ADMM adjoint (20), the stopping criteria and the algorithms' directions; all substantive claims survive, but this is an inference-level, multi-site repair rather than a local transcription fix.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: \IF{ $J(\Pi_E(\varepsilon^{(j)} - \sigma^{(j)}\, D^{(j)} )) > J(\varepsilon^{(j)}) - c \,\sigma^{(j)} |D^{(j)}|^2$ }
\WHILE{ $J(\Pi_E(\varepsilon^{(j)} - \tau^{(k)}\, D^{(j)} ) ) \le J(\varepsilon^{(j)}) - c \,\tau^{(k)} |D^{(j)}|^2$ }
System \eqref{eq:opt_system} can be approximated with a simple direct-adjoint looping (DAL) algorithm, which is essentially a steepest descent along the functional $J$.

issues.failure_explanation: Every Armijo condition in Algorithm 1 is evaluated at the reflected point Pi_E(eps^(j) - tau D^(j)), but the accepted iterate is Pi_E(eps^(j) + sigma^(j+1) D^(j)): the line search certifies sufficient decrease at a point that is then not taken, and the actual step is taken in the opposite direction. With the adjoint as stated in (10b), D^(j) is the gradient (ascent) direction of the reduced cost, so the update increases J; with the adjoint as correctly derived from (8), D^(j) is the descent direction and the Armijo tests examine the ascent point (making the shrinking loop non-terminating). Under either convention one of the two signs is wrong, so as written the algorithm is not the advertised steepest descent. Algorithm 2 inherits the defect through its line 5.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Use the same sign of D^(j) in the Armijo tests and in the accepted update, chosen consistently with the repaired adjoint convention of ISSUE-002 (e.g. keep the tests at -tau D and set eps^(j+1) = Pi_E(eps^(j) - sigma^(j+1) D^(j)) under the stated convention).
issues.overall_effect: Algorithm 1 fails its core contract of monotone decrease of J with Armijo-certified steps (iterates can increase the cost or the line search can stall), and Algorithm 2, which invokes the modified Algorithm 1, inherits the failure.
issues.title: DAL line search certifies the opposite point from the accepted update
issues.why_classification: The defect voids the algorithm's stated descent guarantee, and its repair is not a forced transcription fix because the correct sign is determined only after resolving the derivation inconsistency of ISSUE-002; the eventual edit is localized and no substantive claim is lost.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: where the compactly supported interaction kernel is given by the $C^2$ Wendland function \cite{Wendland1995}
each agent tends to align its state $c_i$ with the states of nearby agents whose intensities are similar
This kind of interaction kernels are standard in the smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) literature

issues.failure_explanation: The C^2 Wendland function cited (Wendland 1995; the SPH literature of Dehnen-Aly 2012) is phi(r) = (4r+1)(1-r)^4, which is positive on [0,1). The printed formula (4r-1)(1-r)^4 equals -1 at r=0 and is negative for r < 1/4, so pairs of agents that are spatially or tonally close repel: the term phi(r_ij)(c_j - c_i) in (1) then pushes c_i away from c_j. This contradicts the model's defining premise of attractive alignment of similar nearby agents and the clustering/consensus behaviour the paper builds on. The source does not print the correct formula, so several sign repairs are compatible with the text and the correction is a mathematical repair of the model definition rather than a forced typo fix.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace (4r-1)(1-r)^4 by the standard nonnegative Wendland C^2 kernel (4r+1)(1-r)^4 on [0,1] (any kernel nonnegative on its support and matching the cited literature restores the model).
issues.overall_effect: Taken at face value, the dynamics (1)-(2) with the kernel (16) is repulsive at short range, so the qualitative attraction, alignment and clustering premises of Sections 1-2 (and the convergence claim of ISSUE-001) fail for the kernel actually printed; the reported numerical behaviour is consistent only with the corrected kernel.
issues.title: Printed interaction kernel is negative near the origin
issues.why_classification: A single-sign correction to the canonical cited kernel restores all model properties, claims and experiments; but since the correct formula is not forced by the source text alone and the erroneous sign inverts the interaction at short range, it is a local mathematical repair rather than a pure typo.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: One should ensure that the compact set $E$ is large enough to allow both global interactions, i.e. $\phi(r_{ij}^\varepsilon)>0$ for any $i,j = 1,\ldots,N$, and no interactions at all, i.e. $\phi(r_{ij}^\varepsilon)=0$ for all $i,j = 1,\ldots,N$.
\frac{\varepsilon_x(t)}{2}\bigl[(x_j-x_i)^2+(y_j-y_i)^2\bigr]
we rescale it so that $(x_i,y_i) \in \Omega := [0,1]^2$ for all pixels

issues.failure_explanation: With the kernel supported in [0,1] and coordinates rescaled to [0,1]^2 (squared diagonal 2), every admissible eps_x >= 2 gives r_ij >= (eps_x/2)*2 >= 2 > 1 for opposite-corner pixels, so phi(r_ij) = 0 and the all-interacting regime required by Remark 1 can never be realized (the same conclusion holds for integer pixel coordinates, where the squared diameter is at least 2). Conversely, complete disconnection requires eps_x >= 2(n-1)^2 for an n x n image under the rescaled coordinates, which exceeds 1100 for images larger than roughly 24 x 24 pixels. Hence the assertion that E = [2,1100]^2 is chosen 'in accordance with' Remark 1 is false for the global-interaction regime (and typically also for the no-interaction regime).

failure_location.quote: In accordance with Remark~\ref{rmk:parameters}, we set $E = [2,1100]^2$ and initialise the control as $\varepsilon_x^{(0)} = \varepsilon_c^{(0)} \equiv 57$ at all discrete times.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Either extend E to include values with (eps_x/2)*d_max^2 + eps_c/2 <= 1 (e.g. eps of order 2/3 on the rescaled domain) and values >= 2(n-1)^2, or weaken the 'in accordance' claim and Remark 1 to the regimes actually reachable.
issues.overall_effect: The narrative that the admissible controls realize both extremal configurations (full interaction, i.e. consensus for small alpha, and zero interaction, i.e. the original image for large alpha), and hence that tuning alpha sweeps the full range of cluster counts, is unsupported for the numerical setup; Remark 1's guideline and the interpretation of the experiments are unreliable in this respect.
issues.title: Choice E=[2,1100]^2 contradicts the stated reachability requirement
issues.why_classification: A local parameter/claim correction; no theorem, algorithm or stated guarantee depends on reachability of the extremal regimes, and the experiments remain valid within the reachable range.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: There exists a saddle point for the functional $L : H^1(\Omega) \times L^2(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^2) \times L^2(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^2) \to \R$ defined in \eqref{eq:cost_tv_regular}.
L(u,v,\mu) = \int_\Omega |v(x)| + \mu(x) \cdot (v(x) - \nabla u(x)) + \frac{\rho}{2} |v(x) - \nabla u(x)|^2 + \frac{\alpha}{2}(u(x)- I(x))^2\ dx.
J(u) \ge C \|u\|_{H^1(\Omega)}^2 - D,
This is the reason why Theorem \ref{thm:saddle_point} is fundamental: it ensures that there is no duality gap.

issues.failure_explanation: Unlike J, whose quadratic gradient term gives H^1 coercivity, L has only linear growth in v (the |v| term) and its quadratic term controls only the difference v - grad u: taking v = grad u along sequences with bounded Integral |grad u| but L^2 norm of grad u diverging (oscillating gradients) leaves L bounded while the H^1 x L^2 norm diverges. So L is not coercive in the primal variables, sublevel sets are not weakly compact, and the direct-method / Ekeland-Temam argument collapses; the analogy with the proof of Theorem 3.1 is invalid. Moreover the statement is false as stated (no hypothesis on I is given beyond the setup): a saddle point (u*,v*,mu*) would force v* = grad u* and K(u*) = L(u*,v*,mu*) <= L(u, grad u, mu*) = K(u) for all u in H^1, i.e. u* would minimize the ROF functional K over H^1; for discontinuous data I (e.g. a characteristic function, which is exactly the digital-image setting, and for which the unique BV minimizer has jumps) no H^1 minimizer exists, hence no saddle point exists. Even granting the paper's standing assumption of continuous I, the proof supplies no valid argument, and H^1 attainment is precisely what fails at edges, the flagship regime of the TV model. The strong-duality display (18), written with attained min and max, inherits the failure.

failure_location.quote: Finally, as in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:existence1}, it is immediate to show coercivity in the primal variables, ensuring that the minimum is attained in a weakly compact set.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: No complete source-supported repair identified; at minimum, a repair must replace the false coercivity argument: either reformulate in BV or add hypotheses guaranteeing that the ROF minimizer lies in H^1 (which excludes the flagship edge-preserving regime), or weaken the theorem to equality of the primal and dual values with dual attainment, proved through an appropriate constraint qualification.
issues.overall_effect: The existence-of-saddle-point guarantee underpinning the TV/ADMM model, invoked explicitly to ensure 'no duality gap' and to justify the ADMM stopping criterion, is unestablished and false in the edge/jump regime that motivates the model; the min-max identity (18) as displayed is unreliable.
issues.title: Saddle-point existence theorem rests on a false coercivity claim and fails for jump data
issues.why_classification: The proof's central premise is demonstrably false (explicit non-coercive sequences), and every supported resolution either excludes the advertised edge-preserving regime, changes the function-space setting in a way the L^2-gradient Lagrangian does not support, or abandons the stated unconditional existence guarantee; no comparable unconditional continuum result survives without essentially new proof architecture.
